title: T1021.008 — Remote Services: Direct Cloud VM Connections
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Remote Services: Direct Cloud VM Connections with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.

steps.title: A token in a public repo
steps.caption: The attacker starts in a laboratory: scanning their own test repository for leaked keys. The scan reports a verified key for the role dev_ci_automation. Direct-connection tools were built for administrators, but a leaked IAM role can turn them into attacker doors.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Enumerate from the outside
steps.caption: Using the stolen role, the attacker lists every running instance from outside the network. One target stands out: a production VM with only a private IP and no SSM agent. CloudTrail quietly records DescribeInstances - normal for a pipeline, odd from this address.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.caption: The attacker asks the control plane to build a tunnel into the private subnet. This API is so rare that many accounts have zero events in their whole history, so the SIEM rule fires a critical page. If someone reads it here, the attack ends before it starts.

steps.title: Push an ephemeral key
steps.caption: One API call pushes a temporary SSH public key onto the instance. The key lives for about 60 seconds and then vanishes on its own. CloudTrail names the identity, the instance, the OS user, and the key fingerprint - everything a defender needs.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: SSH straight through the cloud
steps.caption: The attacker opens an SSH session straight to the private VM. No public port, no VPN, no firewall log. On the machine, sshd writes the accepted-login line with the marker ec2-instance-connect in it - the moment a cloud event becomes a real shell.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Mine and call home
steps.caption: With a shell in hand, the attacker installs a cryptominer and opens a reverse tunnel so they can come back without touching the control plane again. EDR and flow logs see both halves: a strange binary at full CPU, and a steady outbound connection to one host.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: The key evaporates
steps.caption: Sixty seconds later the pushed key expires on its own. The attacker is gone from the SSH layer, but every step lives in CloudTrail, and the open session survives. Cleanup does not hide the story - and the miner keeps burning CPU.

steps.title: How defenders catch this
steps.caption: Four signals, one story: a rare control-plane event, a first-ever key push from a robot role, an OS login line that names the entry path, and a tunnel out. Join them by identity and time and the whole chain sits on one page - no malware reverse engineering required.
